checkpoints: The boundary should carry rank, not score.

Each engine exposes exactly the same shape — a query endpoint returning an ordered list of document ids where position is the only thing that means anything — and the coordinator consumes just that ordering.

The coordinator's own output is fused hits sorted by `rrfScore`, each tagged with its per-source ranks (`bm25Rank`/`vectorRank`, `null` when an engine didn't return the document), so a caller can see whether a document ranked highly because both engines agreed or because only one did.
Failure isolation belongs at exactly this seam: each upstream call is independently guarded, so a dead or slow engine collapses to an empty list and RRF still fuses whatever survives.

Keeping only rank in the contract is the load-bearing decision: raw BM25 and cosine scores are incompatible scales and fragile to normalize, whereas a position contract lets you swap or add engines without touching the fusion layer at all.
The one shared invariant is a canonical document-id space — without it, the same logical document shows up under two different ids and consensus is never detected.
The design centers on exactly ONE `embed(text) -> vector` component that both the index path and the query path must call — never two parallel embedder implementations.
Invariant: exactly one pinned model + version.
Invariant: deterministic output — the same text always yields the same vector, so results are reproducible and cacheable.
Invariant: L2-normalized so cosine reduces to a clean angle comparison.
Invariant: fixed dimensionality that matches the vector column declared in the DB.

Making it the single source of truth structurally kills the model-mismatch bug: because the document vector and the query vector come from the same embedder, they are guaranteed to live in the SAME space.
Validating vector length against the declared dimension right at the write boundary rejects a wrong-dimension vector loudly, instead of letting it silently rot the index.
A model upgrade is a first-class event, not a config edit — the active model + version must be declared explicitly and versioned, and changing it obligates a full re-embed of the store.
BM25 scores each document as the sum, across the query terms it actually contains, of idf(term) times a term-frequency-saturation factor times a length-normalization factor.

In this four-document corpus, `redis` and `failover` each sit in exactly two of the four documents, so both get the same substantial IDF (about 0.69) — neither is a near-universal connector word that would earn an IDF close to zero.

`d1` matches BOTH query terms, so its score sums two separate contributions (idf(redis)*tf plus idf(failover)*tf, roughly 0.72 + 0.72 = 1.4398), while `d4` and `d2` each match only one term and collect only one contribution — that two-term sum is the single biggest reason `d1` tops the ranking.

Between the two single-term matches, `d4` (5 tokens, right around `avgdl`=5.5) edges out `d2` (7 tokens, above average) because the length-normalization term `B*(dl/avgdl)` (B=0.75) damps `d2`'s lone contribution harder than `d4`'s, even though `redis` and `failover` carry identical IDF weight.

Term-frequency saturation (K1=1.2) explains why repetition can't rescue `d2` either: the first occurrence of a term matters most and the tenth adds almost nothing, so no amount of restating `redis` would let `d2` catch up to `d1`'s two-term match.
`d3` matches neither term and doesn't even appear in the hits.
The result is one fused, comparable relevance number per document — not a vote on which words are merely present.
RRF reads only each document's rank in each list and adds `1/(k + rank)` across lists, so nothing but an integer position crosses the boundary between the BM25 scale and the cosine scale.
`doc-3` is in both lists (rank 1 + rank 2), collecting `1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0325`.
`doc-5` leads only one list, collecting `1/61 ≈ 0.0164`.
`doc-3` — the document both engines agree is relevant — wins, even though it was never rank 1 in the vector list.

The raw 12.7-versus-0.91 scores are thrown away on purpose: normalizing two scales that measure different things is fragile, and a single outlier BM25 score would dominate if scores were summed directly.
With `k = 60` the rank-1/rank-2 gap is tiny (`1/61` versus `1/62`) — which is precisely why consensus can outweigh a single first place.
Cosine compares direction (angle) between vectors.
Euclidean compares straight-line distance, which folds in magnitude.
When every vector is L2-normalized to unit length, magnitude becomes constant across all vectors, so cosine and euclidean produce identical rankings.
Therefore the teammate is right for this lesson's setup, where all vectors are normalized.
Cosine is still the correct framing for text similarity because "same topic or not" is a question about direction, not length — that's why it's the default semantic-search operator.

The choice starts to matter the moment vectors aren't normalized: a longer vector can win on euclidean distance purely for its magnitude while cosine still compares topic (a concrete case where the ranking would change).
The safe posture is to L2-normalize and reason in cosine, rather than rely on the two metrics happening to coincide.
k sets how fast a document's contribution decays with rank.

At k = 60, the rank-1 term (1/61) and rank-2 term (1/62) are almost identical — this is why agreement across engines can overcome a small lead within a single engine (the entire reason fusion helps): a document ranked 1st in both lists (1/61 + 1/61) beats a document ranked 1st in only one list (1/61), and even a rank-2-in-both document can outscore a rank-1-single-list document.
Push k toward 1 and rank 1 (1/2) towers over rank 2 (1/3), so one engine's first place dominates the outcome and consensus stops mattering.
Push k very large and every contribution collapses toward equal, so rank stops carrying any information at all.
Both directions destroy the exact thing RRF exists to do: use agreement across position (rank) to tell a genuinely good document apart from one a single engine happens to push to the top.
60 is the empirically validated default from the original Cormack et al. paper.
Only retune k if you have offline relevance data to justify it, and treat any change as a measured ranking-quality experiment rather than a config knob you turn on a whim.
Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query against every vector in the store — O(N), unbearable at millions of vectors.
HNSW is a multi-layer graph whose topmost layers are sparse, allowing long jumps that land near the right neighbourhood.
The lower layers of that graph get progressively denser, refining the exact position.
The walk goes top-down layer by layer — like zooming in on a map — which is why complexity drops to near O(log N) instead of a linear scan.
The trade-off for that speed is that the result is only approximate: HNSW can miss a small fraction of the true neighbours.
ef_search controls how many candidates get visited while walking the graph — visiting more raises recall and latency, visiting fewer lowers both.
To set ef_search for a latency SLA: measure recall on a labeled sample query set and raise ef_search step by step until the recall threshold is just met, then stop.

A too-low ef_search never surfaces as a runtime error — the query still returns normally, but results are silently missing correct neighbours or mis-ranked, catchable only by actively measuring recall.

On the index path, `tokenize()` normalizes text by lowercasing it and splitting on runs of non-alphanumeric characters, so a document containing "Redis" ends up stored under the key `redis` in `this.postings`.

`queryTokenize()` was added later, lives only inside the query handler, and does not reuse `tokenize()` — it merely splits on whitespace and keeps the original case, so the same word can produce a different token depending on which of the two paths processed it.

Because the query token `Redis` and the indexed key `redis` differ only in case, `this.postings.get(term)` returns undefined for a document that genuinely contains the word — the index path and query path have silently drifted out of sync with each other.

A Map lookup miss is not an error condition in JavaScript/TypeScript, it simply returns undefined, so the `if (!posting) continue` guard skips the term without throwing or logging anything, which makes an empty or partial result look like a legitimate "no match" rather than exposing the bug.

Two independent tokenization implementations that are supposed to agree but are edited separately have no crash-shaped failure signature, so an empty result set with zero exceptions is itself the diagnostic clue pointing at a normalization mismatch between index-time and query-time processing, not a BM25 scoring defect.

The correct fix is to delete `queryTokenize()` entirely and call the same `tokenize()` function from `search()`, guaranteeing the index path and query path always normalize text identically and can never diverge again.

After the fix, re-running the query `Redis` (different case than the stored `redis`) should return the previously missing document, and a regression test asserting that index-time and query-time tokenization produce identical tokens for the same input guards against a future edit to only one of the two paths reintroducing the bug.

This failure mode generalizes beyond casing: any asymmetric normalization step applied on only one of the two paths — a stemmer, a stopword filter, synonym expansion — produces the same silent, exception-free recall collapse, so the durable fix is a single shared normalization pipeline rather than a patch for the specific case difference.

"No error, plausible-looking similarity scores, but degraded ranking" is the signature of an embedding-space mismatch rather than a runtime bug - there is no exception or log to chase because cosine similarity always returns a valid float no matter which model produced the vectors.

Each embedding model learns its own coordinate space during training, so a vector produced by one model and a vector produced by a different model do not live in the same space, even when both happen to output the same dimensionality.

Cosine similarity computed between a query vector from one model's space and document vectors from another model's space still executes and returns an arithmetically valid number in a normal-looking range - that number simply carries no semantic meaning.

In this code, EmbeddingService (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) still embeds documents through the nightly reindex job, while this deploy wired SearchService to QueryEmbeddingService (all-MiniLM-L12-v2) for queries, so two different models feed vectors into the same column.

A dimensionality mismatch, meaning different vector lengths, would throw right at insert or comparison time against a fixed-size pgvector column; this bug stays silent specifically because both models happen to output exactly 384 dimensions, so no data-layer check catches the discrepancy.

The fix is to point search() back at the same embedding service used for indexing and remove the extra QueryEmbeddingService dependency entirely, so the index path and query path can never again be wired to two different models by mistake.

If the real goal is to finish migrating to the newer model rather than roll back, the entire documents table must be re-embedded under that model before both paths are pointed at it - a table can never be left holding vectors from two different models at once.

Validating the fix requires more than eyeballing a query: running a known paraphrase pair against its expected ranking confirms the model mismatch was really the cause, and measuring recall on a labelled sample after re-embedding confirms quality actually recovered.

BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent — they shift with term rarity, document length, and index size — while cosine similarity is naturally bounded to [-1, 1], so the two lists don't measure the same kind of quantity to begin with.

Min-max normalizing each list separately to [0, 1] only rescales each list onto the same axis labels; it doesn't make the underlying quantities comparable, so summing the two normalized values produces a number with no real relevance meaning.

A single outlier score in one engine's list — one document scoring far above the rest — stretches that list's min-max range and squashes every other document's normalized value toward zero, letting the outlier dominate the fused sum almost regardless of what the other engine reports.

Because min-max normalization is relative to whatever scores happen to be in the current result set, a shift in one engine's score distribution — reindexing, a corpus change, a scoring tweak — changes a document's normalized value and therefore the fused ranking, even though the document's actual rank and relevance haven't moved at all.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps both failures by fusing on each engine's integer rank rather than its raw score, summing 1/(k+rank) with k = 60 — rank is always comparable across engines no matter what a raw score means or how its distribution shifts, so there's no normalization step left to be fragile.

A constructive code review affirms that combining both engines' signal into one ranking is the right goal, and frames rank-based fusion as the standard, battle-tested way to reach that goal rather than treating the author's intent as wrong.

Regression tests for a score-fusion function should specifically cover an outlier-score scenario and a distribution-shift scenario, asserting that a rank-based fusion keeps the ranking stable in both cases where the min-max version would visibly break.
